To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sorption of E. coli to silt soil and sand was well described by Freundlich and Langmuir isothem models.

sorption of E. coli to soil and sand was well described by the Freundlich isotherm model and that E. coli desorption from sand was nearly complete, whereas E. coli desorbed from soil was only about 15% of that attached.

the number of E coli cells sorbed to soil and sand varied with initial bacterial concentration and sorbent concentration, and were greater to soil than to sand; the Freundlich isotherm model described the observed sorption data best for both sorbent types, with the Langmuir isothem model also describing the data well; and E. coli sorbation to sand was more reversible than sorbation to soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sorption and desorbtion of bacteria to soil particles and sand.
the fate and transport of bacteria, specifically E. coli, in the subsurface environment.
bacterial sorption to soil particles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sorption of E. coli to sand and silt loam was described by Freundlich isotherm with the same exponent but with different coefficients.
E. coli sorbent interactions with silt loam and sand were reversible, and that E. coli partitioned to soil more than to sand.
E. coli sorbs to both soil and silt loam particles in a reversible fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sorption of E. coli onto soil is more efficient and more difficult to reverse than that on sand, which has implications for bacterial transport in the environment.
E. coli sorb to soil and sand particles and that sorption and desoprtion is reversible.

the sorption of E. coli to soil is a complex process that is affected by the quantity of soil, bacterial concentrations, and bacterial cell surface properties, which are affected by the presence or absence of organic matter and other soil components.
The main takeaway from our work is that
E. coli sorbs to sand and soil particles and the extent of sorption is influenced by the initial bacterial concentration, the amount of sorbent added, and the type of sorbent.
E. coli sorbs to both soil and to sand.
the sorption of E. coli to soil particles is an important factor that needs to be considered for predicting the transport and fate of E. coli in the environment.
